lessons.title: Cultural intelligence in everyday work

chapters.title: Welcome to the foundation
paragraphs: Welcome. Cultural understanding supports the work we do across One DHS and One DSD People, Access and Culture. It helps us examine our own culture, learn about the communities we serve, including people with disabilities, and make better decisions with the people affected by them.

Cultural intelligence is an ongoing practice of understanding different perspectives and working effectively across cultural differences. This collection brings together multiple perspectives and approaches, including person-centered practice, psychological safety, intercultural development and attention to implicit bias.

The work can include reflection, learning, planning and adapting. It also involves attention to implicit bias, intercultural development, disability and language access, community knowledge, and the policies and systems that shape participation.

The Intercultural Development Inventory and implicit-association resources can support learning when used appropriately. These tools have different purposes and limits. Participation in this collection does not require sharing assessment results.

Do not use assessment results to rank people or make hiring, promotion or performance decisions. A community description can suggest a question to ask or a barrier to examine; it cannot tell you what an individual believes, needs or prefers.

Knowledge and training never replace direct community engagement, everyday equity conversations and action, or a welcoming, inclusive workplace. Reading and completing a course are starting points; the work happens with people and communities through appropriate engagement.

This learning is voluntary and self-directed. You can pause, read, return to a section, or use a general work example. You do not have to share a personal story. Keep names, case details, personnel information and other private information out of learning activities.

chapters.title: Begin with your own culture
paragraphs: Everyone works from inside cultures, including those treated as the default. Consider the communities and settings that shape your expectations, such as family, faith, profession, DHS, DSD, county and provider offices, and disability and Deaf communities.

A familiar way to communicate, participate or make a decision may feel neutral to us while creating a barrier for someone else. Notice your expectations and assumptions, consider what shaped them, and ask what the situation and the people affected actually need.

Your culture meets the cultures of the communities you serve, including people with disabilities. Culture, disability, language, geography, opportunity and other parts of life may shape how a process works for someone, and those connections are not the same for everyone. So look at how a rule or process works where they meet, without adding up anyone's identities. A community description, a person's disability or a name cannot tell you what that individual believes, needs or prefers. Ask the person what matters to them and listen to their answer.

For leaders, the questions apply equally to policy, programs and resources, and to hiring, supervision, development and workplace culture. What assumptions are built into a decision or routine? Who can use it, whose voice may be missing, and who has the authority to change it?

chapters.title: Choose your starting point
paragraphs: From there, you can begin with a situation in your work. Perhaps you are revising a service invitation, considering a program or resource decision, reviewing a hiring step, or making a team practice more inclusive. Name the purpose, the decision that is still open and the people who may be affected. Use a general example here.

You can also begin with a community or cultural brief. Choose one that helps you learn about a history, contribution, place or resource. Treat it as a source of better questions, not a description of an individual, and learn from the people affected.

Both paths can lead to the same practical questions, including who will tell you whether your work helped them. You do not need to read every brief or finish every course. Choose what is relevant, and return to a different starting point whenever it helps.

chapters.title: Connect learning to the right tools
paragraphs: Different tools help with different parts of the work. The DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit helps you examine a decision, affected people, evidence and options. Check current DHS policy and the Toolkit user guide, and consult the responsible office or your equity director about whether an Equity Scan or another required analysis applies. A learning activity does not replace that process.

The National CLAS Standards help you consider culturally and linguistically appropriate services. Accessibility resources help you examine whether communication, meetings and materials can be used. Community engagement resources help you plan meaningful participation while a decision can still be influenced and explain what happened afterward.

Person-centered practice begins with the person's own goals and choices. Charting the LifeCourse is a promising way to consider a person's vision and supports when that fits the work. If you have an Intercultural Development Inventory development plan, you may choose to connect a goal from your debrief to your own learning. Like cultural intelligence measures, it is never used here for hiring, promotion, ratings or reviews. You can use this collection without taking an assessment or sharing your results.

These resources serve different purposes. Use those that fit your question, follow their own instructions and current requirements, and avoid putting personal or case information into an informal learning activity. Before acting, name your assumptions; while acting, notice what happens; afterward, check what needs to change.

chapters.title: Try a next step
paragraphs: Imagine a team is revising an invitation to a planning opportunity. The team has read a community brief and found a resource that might help people participate. The decision is still open. What would you do next?

Choose the resource for everyone associated with the community; ask affected people what would make participation workable and check the available options and decision process; or finish the invitation because the team has already completed its reading. Pause the video now and choose your response in the activity before continuing.

Asking people and checking the options keeps their experience and choices central. It also helps the team understand what it can change, what support may be needed and who is responsible. When you do not yet know what someone wants, do not guess. Prepare options and let people choose. Reading can prepare a better question, but it cannot answer that question for the people affected.

chapters.title: Continue with care
paragraphs: Use the collection's Learn, Explore and Apply sections in the order that helps you. If you are unsure, begin by reflecting on your own culture and the situation you are working on. Follow an existing lesson for deeper practice, explore an available brief, or open a relevant tool. For substantive matters concerning Native American individuals, communities or Tribal Nations, follow the standing direction to defer to the Office of Indian Affairs and the DHS offices responsible for Tribal relations and consultation. General learning and engagement do not replace an applicable government-to-government process.

Choose one next step: ask a better question, check an access option, bring a concern to the person with authority, or plan how to listen and report back. A small, responsible action can connect learning with better experiences for people and a more welcoming workplace.

lessons.question: Imagine a team is revising an invitation to a planning opportunity. The team has read a community brief and found a resource that might help people participate. The decision is still open. What would you do next?

choices.text: Choose the resource for everyone associated with the community.
choices.feedback: A resource can be useful, but a community brief does not establish what every individual wants or needs.

choices.text: Ask affected people what would make participation workable and check the available options and decision process.
choices.feedback: This connects learning to the people affected, their choices, and an honest check of options and responsibilities.

choices.text: Finish the invitation because the team has already completed its reading.
choices.feedback: Reading can help prepare questions, but it does not replace appropriate engagement or reveal whether the invitation works for people.

lessons.title: Read a source with care

chapters.title: Separate the question from the answer
paragraphs: Research can deepen your understanding, especially when you keep track of what a source actually supports. Start by naming the claim you want to check. A broad question such as how a community understands disability contains many different questions about people, settings, experiences and time periods.

A more useful question might be: what did this particular study find among the people who participated, and what does it leave unanswered? That wording helps you avoid turning a limited finding into a description of everyone.
Consider more than one possible explanation before drawing a conclusion. A source can help you ask a better question, but it does not answer that question about an individual.

chapters.title: Look at the source and its scope
paragraphs: When you open a source, look for who produced it, what it examined, when it was published and how it reached its conclusions. A historical account, a person's own story, an organization's description of its services and a research study can each contribute something different.

Consider a study about one group of participants in one location. Its findings may help you prepare questions, but they do not automatically describe people in Minnesota or someone you meet at work. Keep the location, participants, topic and limits attached to the finding.

Look closely at labels. Race, ethnicity, nation, language and culture are different things, and sources may blur them. Disability and service categories have histories of their own. Ask what sits behind a label and who chose it; when it matters, ask people what they call themselves.

A person's story is valuable as that person's account. It does not have to represent an entire community to matter. An organization can describe its own services, but a listing does not establish that a service is available to a particular person today.

chapters.title: Keep dates attached to changing information
paragraphs: Dates matter in different ways. A historical event may be stable, while a telephone number, program schedule, leadership role or eligibility detail may change. Look for when the information was checked and whether the original source provides a more recent update.

Sometimes two sources use similar words for different events. An organization may have begun informal work before incorporation or before opening a public location. Before choosing a date, find out which event the source means. If the evidence still conflicts, keep the uncertainty visible rather than choosing the most convenient answer.

For practical use, avoid copying a contact detail into several places without a way to keep it current. A link to the organization's own information may be more useful than a schedule copied long ago.

chapters.title: Distinguish evidence from an inference
paragraphs: Imagine a source says that participants in a study described difficulty reaching a service during its opening hours. That is a finding about the participants and the study. It does not establish that every member of a community faces the same barrier, or that changing the hours is the only useful response.

You could use the finding to ask whether the hours work for people using your process, what alternatives are available and who can make a change. That is an application informed by evidence. It is still something to examine, not a conclusion the study has already made for your workplace.

Now suppose a report says that people in a program often missed appointments. Before you read that as culture, stop and ask: What else could explain this: schedule, transport, cost, an agency rule? What does our own system assume? It may assume a car, a daytime phone, time off work, or a form read in English.
Consider what may be personal, cultural, structural, or related to disability and access. Write down more than one possible explanation before choosing one, and check with the people affected.

chapters.title: Try a source question
paragraphs: Suppose a summary describes a study in another state and gives no information about whether people in your setting were included. Which response is most careful? Treat it as a rule for everyone with that identity; discard it because it comes from elsewhere; or read the original source, retain its limits and use it to prepare questions rather than predict individual needs. Pause the video now and choose your response in the activity before continuing.

The third response keeps the useful learning and the limits together. It gives the source an appropriate role without making it answer a question it did not investigate. Those questions can include what else might explain the finding, and what sits behind its labels.

chapters.title: Carry the source forward
paragraphs: When you use a fact in your own work, keep a usable reference to the original source and the date where that matters. Make it possible for a colleague to see how you reached the statement. If a detail remains uncertain, describe what is known and what needs checking.

For your next step, choose one non-sensitive statement you are considering using. Ask: what exactly supports this, what is its scope, what sits behind its labels, what else could explain it, and what would I need to check before relying on it? That habit helps research improve your work without giving it more certainty than it has.

lessons.question: Suppose a summary describes a study in another state and gives no information about whether people in your setting were included. Which response is most careful?

choices.text: Treat it as a rule for everyone with that identity.
choices.feedback: The study's participants and scope do not establish the needs of every individual.

choices.text: Discard it because it comes from elsewhere.
choices.feedback: A study from elsewhere may still offer useful questions when its scope is kept clear.

choices.text: Read the original source, retain its limits and use it to prepare questions rather than predict individual needs.
choices.feedback: This preserves both the useful learning and the limits of what the source can support.

lessons.title: Make a useful connection

chapters.title: Move from a resource to a purpose
paragraphs: An available community page may mention organizations, publications and other starting points. Before using a resource, name what you hope the connection will accomplish. Are you seeking background reading, learning about an institution, checking a program or preparing for an appropriate conversation?

These purposes are different. A media outlet can offer reporting and perspectives. A historical institution can help you explore records. A service organization may offer a particular program. None of those roles automatically makes an organization the representative of every person in a community.

chapters.title: Ask the person and check the resource
paragraphs: Return to a planning conversation. A participant says that someone they trust might help them prepare. You have just read about a community organization and think it might be useful.

Begin by asking whom the participant wants involved and what role they want that person to have. How they decide, and with whom, is theirs to tell you. Do not substitute a resource mentioned on a page for their preference. If they want information about an organization, check its current official information and explain what you have and have not confirmed.

Who is in the room can shape what people feel able to say. Family, interpreters and providers may affect a conversation, and people may hold back from someone who has a say in their services. Offer a private option, more time and more than one way to answer.

Avoid promising a service, appointment or outcome before it is confirmed through the appropriate process. A website may describe a program without establishing availability or suitability for this person. Follow the applicable consent and information-sharing requirements before making a connection that involves personal details.

chapters.title: Let stories deepen understanding
paragraphs: Individual profiles can show how people have shaped science, civic life, the arts, disability advocacy or local institutions. Read them as specific lives, with their own circumstances and contributions.

Ask what the story helps you notice. Perhaps it draws your attention to a rule that shaped access or to an institution that people built together. Then return to your work and ask what you need to understand there. Avoid assuming that someone today shares the featured person's views or experiences.

Images also need context. A portrait shows a particular person. A photograph of a building or neighborhood shows a place. Read the caption so you know what you are seeing, and do not treat a contextual image as a portrait or as a complete picture of a community.

chapters.title: Respect the right relationship and process
paragraphs: Some work requires a particular relationship and process. For matters involving Native American individuals, communities or Tribal Nations, follow One DSD's standing direction to defer to the Office of Indian Affairs and the DHS offices responsible for Tribal relations and consultation. For matters involving Tribal Nations, general community information or a listening activity does not replace the appropriate government-to-government process.
In other settings too, clarify who can advise, who decides and what participation can influence. A useful invitation explains the purpose, available choices and next steps honestly.
Consider who is being asked to adapt and who has the power to change the process. Look at policies, timelines, formats and access as well as individual communication.

The institution and people with more power should examine what they can change, so the people served do not carry the entire burden of adapting. Follow applicable rights and duties. A person may communicate by speech, writing, a communication device, an interpreter or a chosen supporter.

chapters.title: Try a practical choice
paragraphs: You read about a promising organization on an available community page. A colleague suggests sending a participant's details immediately so the organization can contact them. What should you do first? Send the details because the organization appears relevant; ask about the participant's wishes, verify the resource and follow the applicable information-sharing process; or assume that community connections can never be useful. Pause the video now and choose your response in the activity before continuing.

The second response keeps the opportunity and the person's choice together. It also recognizes that information sharing and referral procedures need to be followed. The community page is a starting point, not permission to disclose information.

chapters.title: Close the loop
paragraphs: After an agreed next step, restate it. Say who will do what, by when, and when the person can expect an update. If an option does not work, explain what happened and consider another appropriate route. Do not leave a person with an unconfirmed promise.

Check whether your explanation was understood in a way that works for the person. Offer more than one way to respond, including a communication device or a chosen supporter. The purpose is to check and improve the explanation, not to test the person.

Choose one general process from your work. What makes a resource connection useful there: a clearer purpose, a current contact, a person's consent, an accessible way to respond, a restated next step, or a change our own process could make? Name one improvement you can raise with the right person or office.

That is how a collection becomes useful in everyday work: a source helps you understand, a question keeps the person's choices central, and a clear next step turns learning into action. None of it replaces direct community engagement, everyday equity conversations and action, or a welcoming, inclusive workplace.

lessons.question: You read about a promising organization on an available community page. A colleague suggests sending a participant's details immediately so the organization can contact them. What should you do first?

choices.text: Send the details because the organization appears relevant.
choices.feedback: A relevant resource does not itself provide permission to share personal information.

choices.text: Ask about the participant's wishes, verify the resource and follow the applicable information-sharing process.
choices.feedback: This respects the person's choice while checking the resource and appropriate process.

choices.text: Assume that community connections can never be useful.
choices.feedback: A connection may be useful when it fits the person's wishes and the appropriate process is followed.
